subjects.name: Conductors and Wiring Methods
defs: A conductor with no covering or electrical insulation.
A conductor or group of conductors that serves as a common connection for two or more circuits.
A factory assembly of two or more insulated conductors having an overall covering.
A material, usually in the form of a wire, cable, or busbar, suitable for carrying electric current.
A flexible conductor assembly with insulation, often with a jacket, intended for temporary or movable use.
A conductor encased within material of composition or thickness not recognized by the NEC as electrical insulation.
A conductor encased within material recognized as electrical insulation.
A conductor consisting of a single wire of solid metal rather than strands.
A conductor composed of a group of wires twisted together or otherwise combined to form a single conductor.
A multiplier applied to ampacity values when more than three current-carrying conductors are installed in a raceway or cable without maintaining spacing for heat dissipation.
The ampacity of a conductor adjusted for conditions of use, as determined by the applicable ampacity tables and correction/adjustment factors.
The temperature of the air or medium surrounding a conductor or equipment.
The maximum current, in amperes, that a conductor can carry continuously under the conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating.
A load where the maximum current is expected to continue for 3 hours or more; conductors and overcurrent devices for continuous loads are sized with higher loading requirements.
A conductor used to carry electric current under normal operating conditions.
An open or ventilated environment that allows for heat dissipation and air flow around an installed conductor.
A multiplier applied to ampacity values when the ambient temperature differs from the temperature used in the ampacity table.
The maximum temperature rating associated with equipment terminations, which can limit the ampacity of conductors connected to that equipment.
An enclosure for conductors, connections, or devices, intended to provide protection and facilitate access.
The volume occupied by conductors, devices, fittings, and equipment grounds within a box, limited to prevent overcrowding and overheating.
A fitting installed at the end of a raceway or in a box to provide a smooth, rounded edge to protect conductors from abrasion.
A short length of conduit or threaded nipple used to connect two boxes or enclosures through a wall or partition.
A separate portion of a conduit or tubing system that provides access to the interior and facilitates pulling or changes in direction.
An accessory such as a locknut, bushing, connector, or coupling used to connect or terminate wiring components.
An enclosure for use in underground systems that is intended to be accessed by hand rather than by persons entering the enclosure.
A box used to enclose conductor splices or connections.
A fitting used to secure a raceway or fitting to a box or enclosure, typically in conjunction with a bushing or connector.
A box used to provide a mounting point for receptacles, switches, luminaires, or other equipment.
A box used to facilitate pulling conductors through a raceway system, without necessarily enclosing splices.
A unit or assembly of units or sections and associated fittings forming a rigid structural system used to securely fasten or support cables and raceways.
A raceway of circular cross section with additional requirements for wall thickness and installation.
The percentage or space occupied by conductors in a raceway, limited to allow heat dissipation and ease of pulling.
A thin-wall steel raceway that is not threaded and is installed with couplings and connectors.
A pliable, nonmetallic raceway of circular cross section intended for use in concealed, dry locations and installed with fittings.
A circular metal raceway of flexible construction formed without seams, used where flexibility is needed without a liquidtight requirement.
A steel raceway of intermediate wall thickness, threaded or used with fittings, heavier than EMT and lighter than RMC.
A flexible metal raceway covered with a liquidtight, nonmetallic jacket, used where flexibility and liquidtight protection are required.
A nonmetallic raceway of circular cross section, available for use in exposed or concealed locations depending on type and installation conditions.
An enclosed channel designed expressly for holding wires, cables, or busbars, with additional functions as permitted in the NEC.
A thick-wall threaded metal raceway of circular cross section, suitable for general use in harsh environments.
A sheet metal enclosure with hinged or removable covers, designed for holding insulated conductors and cables, used as a wiring method.
A factory assembly of insulated conductors in a flexible metallic enclosure, with an internal bonding strip or means, used in specific locations.
A factory assembly of one or more insulated conductors enclosed within an armor of interlocking metal tape or a smooth or corrugated metallic sheath.
A factory assembly of two or more insulated conductors enclosed within a nonmetallic jacket, commonly used in residential wiring.
A single-conductor or multiconductor assembly for service-entrance or feeder use, with or without an outer covering, as specified for the cable type.
A factory assembly of two or more insulated conductors with a nonmetallic jacket, suitable for installation in cable trays and other approved locations.
A moisture-resistant, corrosion-resistant cable for use underground, including direct burial, with an overall nonmetallic jacket.
A moisture-resistant cable suitable for use underground, including direct burial, for service-entrance or feeder applications.

subjects.name: Overcurrent Protection
defs: The largest amount of current capable of being delivered at a point on the system during a short-circuit condition.
The current delivered at a point on the system during a short circuit or ground fault condition.
The highest current at rated voltage that a device is intended to interrupt under standard test conditions.
Any current in excess of the rated current of equipment or the ampacity of a conductor.
A device used to protect conductors and equipment from overcurrent by opening the circuit.
An excessive current in a circuit that occurs within its normal ampacity rating.
An accidental connection of relatively low impedance between two points of different potential in an electric circuit.
The highest prospective short-circuit current that equipment can withstand at its rated voltage without sustaining damage.
A fuse having an insulating tube with metallic ferrules or blades at each end to which the fusible element is attached.
A fuse that reduces the let-through current during high fault currents by interrupting the circuit in less than a half-cycle.
A fuse containing two elements, one for overload protection and one for short-circuit protection.
An overcurrent protective device with a circuit-opening fusible part that is heated and severed by the passage of overcurrent through it.
A device for holding a fuse and connecting it into an electrical circuit.
A fuse with a screw shell and contact and an adapter or other body for use in Edison-base fuseholders.
A fuse that has a delay in opening to allow for temporary inrush currents while still opening on sustained overloads.
A plug fuse with a rejection feature that prevents interchange with fuses of different ampere ratings when used with the proper adapter.
A circuit breaker trip unit that allows adjustment of the trip current or time settings.
A device designed to open and close a circuit by non-automatic means and to open automatically on overcurrent.
A circuit breaker using solid-state components to sense current and provide adjustable trip functions.
The portion of a circuit breaker trip unit that operates with no intentional time delay on short-circuit currents.
A circuit breaker assembled as an integral unit in a supportive and enclosing housing of insulating material.
A switch assembled as an integral unit in a supportive and enclosing housing of insulating material, not providing automatic overcurrent protection.
A device intended to provide limited overcurrent protection for specific equipment or internal circuits, not generally for branch circuit or feeder conductor protection.
A circuit breaker that uses a bimetallic element for overload protection and a magnetic trip for short-circuit protection.
The rating in amperes of the overcurrent protective device, which shall not exceed the conductor ampacity unless otherwise permitted.
Overcurrent protection provided for branch circuits in accordance with the ampere rating and conductor ampacity requirements.
Requirement that overcurrent protection be provided to protect conductors from overcurrent in accordance with their ampacity.
Overcurrent protection provided for feeders to protect conductors and meet system requirements.
NEC provisions specifying where OCPDs must be located for accessibility and protection.
Permission to use the next higher standard overcurrent device rating where conductor ampacity does not correspond to a standard rating and stated limits are met.
Overcurrent protection provided at the service entrance to protect the service conductors.
Conductors permitted to be protected by the overcurrent device of the feeder or larger conductor in accordance with tap rules.
An analysis of overcurrent protective devices to verify selective coordination for specified fault currents.
A property of an overcurrent device where it interrupts a fault current before its first peak, reducing let-through current and energy.
An overcurrent protective device system where each device has an interrupting rating equal to or greater than the available fault current at its location.
The thermal energy let-through by an overcurrent device during fault interruption, used in evaluating damage to conductors and equipment.
The current passed through a current-limiting overcurrent device during a fault, less than the available fault current.
Localization of an overcurrent condition to restrict outages to the circuit or equipment affected, accomplished by the selection and application of overcurrent protective devices.
A combination of two overcurrent devices in series that allows the downstream device to have a lower interrupting rating under tested conditions.
The total time from the beginning of a fault until the overcurrent device opens and interrupts the fault current.

subjects.name: Grounding and Bonding
defs: The conductive mass of the earth, which is taken as zero potential.
A conductor used to connect the non-current-carrying metal parts of equipment, raceways, and other enclosures to the system grounded conductor.
A system or circuit conductor that is intentionally grounded.
An electrical system in which at least one conductor or point is intentionally connected to earth.
The process of connecting electrical systems or equipment to earth or to a conductive body that serves in place of earth.
A conductor used to connect equipment or the grounded circuit of a wiring system to a grounding electrode or electrodes.
A system or circuit grounded directly to earth without the insertion of any resistor or impedance.
A conductor not intentionally connected to ground in a grounded electrical system.
An electrical system with no conductor intentionally grounded.
Connected together to establish electrical continuity and a common conductive path.
The permanent joining of metallic parts to form an electrically conductive path that ensures electrical continuity and the capacity to conduct safely any current likely to be imposed.
A conductor used to connect metallic parts to provide electrical continuity.
A path that provides unbroken conductivity for fault current.
The connection between two or more portions of the equipment grounding conductor system.
The connection between the grounded circuit conductor and the equipment grounding conductor at the service.
The practice of bonding metal raceways, enclosures, and cabinets together and to the grounding system.
A conductor installed on the supply side of a service or separately derived system to ensure electrical continuity and conductivity.
The connection between the grounded circuit conductor and the supply-side bonding jumper, or the equipment grounding conductor, or both, at a separately derived system.
A grounding electrode consisting of at least 20 feet of bare copper conductor encased in concrete in direct contact with earth.
A ring encircling a building or structure, in direct contact with earth, consisting of at least 20 feet of bare copper conductor.
A conducting object through which a direct connection to earth is established.
A conductor used to connect the system grounded conductor or the equipment to a grounding electrode or to a point on the grounding electrode system.
All grounding electrodes that are bonded together and used for grounding a system or equipment.
A grounding electrode that is manufactured and installed for the purpose of establishing a ground connection.
A metal water pipe in direct contact with earth for 10 feet or more that may be used as a grounding electrode.
A metal plate buried in the earth to serve as a grounding electrode.
A metal rod driven into the ground to serve as a grounding electrode.
An intentionally constructed path of low impedance to facilitate the operation of overcurrent protective devices during a ground fault.
Current that flows from an ungrounded conductor to ground, ground return, or equipment during a ground fault.
The connection of the grounded conductor to equipment enclosures and to the grounding electrode at specific points.
A system grounded through an impedance, typically to limit ground-fault current.
The common point on a star-connected transformer or generator winding.
A system grounded through a resistor to limit ground-fault current.
An electrical source, other than a service, with no direct electrical connection to supply conductors originating in another system.
The conductors and equipment for delivering energy from the serving utility to the premises wiring system.
The conductors from the service point to the service disconnecting means.
The point of connection between the facilities of the serving utility and the premises wiring.
A device that opens a circuit under predetermined overcurrent conditions.
The path of a ground fault from equipment to the electrical supply source via the equipment grounding conductor.
The maximum voltage a grounded structure may attain relative to a distant grounding point during a ground fault.
Protection intended to reduce the risk of electric shock to people.
A system intended to provide protection of equipment from damaging line-to-ground fault currents.
The path taken by ground-fault current to return to the source of supply.
A continuous conductive path for fault current from the point of a ground fault to the electrical supply source.
A conductive path with low resistance and reactance that allows large fault currents to flow.
The voltage between a person's feet at two different points in the earth near an energized object.
The voltage between an energized object and a person's feet when the person is touching the object.

subjects.name: GFCI and AFCI
defs: A GFCI that trips when ground-fault current is between four and six milliamperes.
A difference between current in the ungrounded and grounded conductors of a circuit.
A circuit breaker that provides ground-fault protection for an entire branch circuit.
A receptacle incorporating integral ground-fault circuit interrupter protection.
An unintentional electrical path between an energized conductor and ground or grounded parts.
A device that de-energizes a circuit upon detecting current imbalance between conductors.
A neutral-to-ground connection on the load side of a GFCI that prevents the device from tripping.
Small unintended current flowing from an energized conductor to ground through insulation.
Protection intended to reduce the risk of electric shock to people.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles in bathroom locations.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles in boathouses and similar locations.
GFCI protection provided to downstream receptacles connected to the load side of a GFCI device.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles supplied by temporary wiring during construction or maintenance.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles in attached or detached garages.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles serving kitchen countertops.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles installed outdoors.
NEC requirement for GFCI protection of receptacles in unfinished basement areas.
An unintended arc produced by current flowing through an unintentional path.
A device that de-energizes a circuit upon detecting a potentially dangerous electrical arc.
An AFCI that provides protection against parallel arcs in branch circuit and feeder wiring.
An AFCI that provides protection against both series and parallel arc faults.
Protection intended to mitigate arc faults that could ignite combustible materials.
An arc between two conductors of opposite polarity or between conductor and ground.
An arc in series with a conductor due to a break or loose connection.
NEC requirement to provide AFCI protection when extending or modifying branch circuits in dwelling units.
A circuit breaker providing arc-fault protection for an entire branch circuit.
Specific circuits or locations exempt from AFCI protection under NEC provisions.
A circuit breaker providing both ground-fault and arc-fault protection.
NEC requirement for AFCI protection of bedroom branch circuits in dwelling units.
NEC areas beyond bedrooms requiring AFCI protection in most dwelling unit circuits.
A branch circuit supplying receptacle outlets, often subject to AFCI protection requirements.
A receptacle-type AFCI device that protects downstream branch-circuit wiring when installed at the first outlet.
GFCI protection applied at the breaker to protect an entire branch circuit.
GFCI protection considerations for receptacles in damp but not wet locations.
NEC provisions that address GFCI or AFCI protection requirements for existing installations.
A miswiring condition where supply conductors land on the load terminals, leaving the GFCI without line power.
GFCI protection used for cord-and-plug connected portable appliances in required locations.
GFCI protection applied to a receptacle outlet to protect users from ground faults.
NEC requirement to provide GFCI or AFCI protection when replacing receptacles in certain locations.
GFCI protection required for receptacles in wet locations due to shock hazard.

subjects.name: Load Calculations
defs: The total load placed on a branch circuit as determined by NEC calculation rules.
The load value determined by applying NEC rules for sizing conductors or equipment.
The total rating of all equipment and outlets connected to a circuit or system.
A load where maximum current is expected to continue for three hours or more.
The portion of connected load expected to be used at the same time under normal conditions.
The total calculated load supplied by a feeder to one or more branch circuits or loads.
The amount of electric power or current consumed by connected equipment or circuits.
A load where maximum current is not expected to continue for three hours or more.
The total calculated load supplied by the service conductors to the premises.
The calculated load for an electric clothes dryer in a dwelling per NEC demand rules.
A unit-area lighting load applied to habitable space in a dwelling per NEC tables.
The larger of heating or air-conditioning load used when sizing dwelling service per NEC rules.
An alternate method for dwelling service sizing using specific NEC demand factors.
Outlets not part of small appliance or laundry circuits counted for load calculation in dwellings.
The load of permanently installed appliances in a dwelling not counted under other circuits.
A required dwelling branch circuit serving the laundry area receptacle outlet per NEC rules.
The calculated load for an electric cooking range or cooktop in a dwelling per NEC tables.
Dwelling branch circuits serving receptacles in kitchen and dining areas per NEC requirements.
A type of assembly with multiple receptacles calculated per NEC length-based rules.
Loads from motors calculated with NEC requirements including full-load current and adjustments.
A unit-area lighting load applied to occupancies other than dwellings per NEC tables.
An alternate method for certain non-dwelling loads using approved NEC demand factors.
Load for general-use receptacles calculated with specific NEC rules for non-dwelling occupancies.
Calculated load for exterior lighting in non-dwelling applications per NEC requirements.
A calculated load for show windows based on linear length per NEC rules.
A minimum load assigned to each sign or outline lighting outlet per NEC requirements.
A calculated load for track lighting based on length or specified minimums per NEC rules.
A factor applied to fixed appliance loads when more than four are present in a dwelling.
A factor applied to cooking ranges or ovens based on number and rating per NEC tables.
The ratio of maximum demand to total connected load expressed as a percent or decimal.
Demand factors reduce calculated load while ampacity adjustments address conductor temperature or bundling.
The ratio of sum of individual demands to maximum system demand for a group of loads.
A factor applied to electric clothes dryer loads in dwellings per NEC demand tables.
A reduced percentage applied to general lighting loads based on occupancy and NEC tables.
A reduction applied to the neutral conductor load based on unbalanced load calculations.
A factor applied to certain receptacle loads to account for non-coincident use per NEC rules.
The total load used to size service conductors and equipment after applying NEC rules.
Multiple loads grouped together when applying NEC demand factors or sizing equipment.
The smallest allowable service ampacity for a given occupancy per NEC minimum requirements.
Sizing the neutral based on maximum unbalanced load with permitted reductions per NEC rules.
The required ampacity of service conductors based on the calculated service load.
The conductors from the service point to the service disconnecting means per NEC requirements.
The minimum rating of service disconnecting means based on calculated service load.
Overcurrent protection for service conductors sized per NEC ampacity requirements.
The ampere rating of the service equipment as determined by load calculation per NEC rules.
